title: Volume

findings.finding: The demonstrations do not expose the left-right reversal needed for an asymmetric back view.
findings.breakdown: Copying the front view unchanged succeeds in both worked examples and the visibly symmetric guided solids, but puts the vertical edge on the wrong side in p4-q1-a. The same mistake affects the asymmetric ends later in p4-q1.
findings.checked: Checked all drawing-prisms teaching. Neither worked example nor the visible guided prompts contrast an asymmetric front with its back. The reversal mentioned in a hidden answer specification is not student-visible teaching.
findings.assumptions: Students keep the solid upright when moving from its front to its back.

repair.proposal: Before p4-q1-a, add: “Keep the solid upright and imagine walking round to its back. The vertical edge on the left in the front view appears on the right in the back view. Sketch both end views to show this reversal.”

findings.doneWhen: An asymmetric front/back pair explicitly demonstrates the reversal before independent practice.

findings.finding: Compare parallel sections at different heights in the existing cone.
findings.breakdown: The run distinguishes retaining a circular shape from retaining the same size.
findings.checked: The cone sections are circles decreasing in size towards the apex. These qualitative comparisons require only the cross-section teaching already supplied; no numerical similarity calculation is needed.

repair.proposal: Append to p12-q1 under its existing instruction, adding only: “Predict before drawing.” g. Draw a section of the cone in part e parallel to its base, one-quarter of the way from the base to the apex. h. Repeat halfway from the base to the apex. i. Repeat three-quarters of the way from the base to the apex. Expected: circles decreasing in size from g to i. Follow with unpatterned part j: Draw a section of the pentagonal prism in part c parallel to its base, halfway along the prism. Expected: a pentagon identical in shape and size to the base. The run varies slice height while keeping the cone and cutting direction fixed.

findings.doneWhen: Three cone sections and the contrasting prism section follow the existing parts.

findings.finding: Compare the effects of changing base area and prism height on volume.
findings.breakdown: Changing one factor at a time exposes how each contributes to V = Ah.
findings.checked: All proposed volumes are correct. The questions use the existing base-area-given method, and the supplied practice contains no comparable consecutive run.
findings.assumptions: A denotes base area and h denotes perpendicular prism height.

repair.proposal: Append after p16-q1-i under the existing instruction. Add only: “Predict how each volume compares with the previous one before calculating.” j. A = 6 cm², h = 4 cm. Answer: 24 cm³. k. A = 12 cm², h = 4 cm. Answer: 48 cm³. l. A = 12 cm², h = 8 cm. Answer: 96 cm³. m. A = 6 cm², h = 8 cm. Answer: 48 cm³. Follow with unpatterned part n: A = 7.5 cm², h = 3 cm. Answer: 22.5 cm³. Each consecutive patterned part changes one factor while keeping the other fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The four-part run and one unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing volume instruction.

findings.finding: The diameter-given example substitutes radius 7 m without deriving it from the labelled 14 m.
findings.breakdown: The working introduces a different length in the radius position without modelling the diameter-to-radius decision.
findings.checked: The circle-area review rehearses this conversion, but the worked-example standard still requires a written connection when the labelled length changes before substitution. No connecting line appears in p24-example-right.
findings.assumptions: Calculator availability does not affect the missing decision.

repair.proposal: Before the volume substitution, insert: “r = d ÷ 2 = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 m.”

findings.doneWhen: The example derives 7 m before substituting it.

findings.finding: The unknown-radius cylinder task is repeated with unchanged mathematical givens.
findings.breakdown: Both tasks ask for radius x with volume 615.8 cm³ and height 16 cm. Their cylinder diagrams encode the same task, with no explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared both complete parts, their group instructions and diagram specifications. The different generic instructions do not change the required task. The replacement gives sqrt(1005.3 ÷ (20π)) ≈ 4.0 cm.
findings.assumptions: A calculator is available for the inverse-radius calculation.

repair.proposal: Keep p27-q8-a. In p28-q13-c, change the volume to 1005.3 cm³ and height to 20 cm, retaining radius x cm. Answer: x ≈ 4.0 cm.

findings.doneWhen: The later cylinder retains its structure with different givens and a matching answer.

findings.finding: Explain why an inscribed cylinder occupies the same percentage of every cube.
findings.breakdown: The task generalises the existing numerical comparison through the two taught volume formulas.
findings.checked: For cube side s > 0, the cylinder has radius s/2 and height s. Its volume is πs³/4, while the cube's volume is s³. Their ratio is π/4, giving 25π%, approximately 78.5%. The formulas and the inscribed configuration are already available.
findings.assumptions: The cylinder fits upright with diameter and height equal to the cube side. Elementary algebra is prior knowledge; a calculator is needed only for the decimal percentage.

repair.proposal: After p28-q12, offer: “A cylinder fits exactly inside a cube, with its circular ends touching all four sides of the corresponding square faces. Would a larger cube change the percentage occupied by the cylinder? Justify your answer for a cube of side s > 0.” Expected answer: r = s/2 and h = s, so cylinder volume = πs³/4 and cube volume = s³. The percentage is always 25π%, approximately 78.5%.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the independence from cube size, including the condition s > 0.

findings.finding: Converting 2 m³ to cm³ is repeated three times, including consecutive identical practice parts.
findings.breakdown: The later parts repeat the complete quantity, destination and operation without an explicit comparison or retrieval purpose.
findings.checked: Compared all three prompts and their group instructions. No diagrams or additional givens distinguish them. Both replacement conversions are correct.
findings.assumptions: The repetitions have no instructional purpose beyond the supplied instructions.

repair.proposal: Keep p30-guided-b. Change p31-q4-b to “3 m³ to cm³”, answer 3,000,000 cm³. Change p31-q4-c to “4 m³ to cm³”, answer 4,000,000 cm³.

findings.doneWhen: Both later copies retain the conversion structure with different starting values.

findings.finding: Two later capacity exercise parts repeat unchanged tasks from the supplementary drills.
findings.breakdown: The conversion 2000 mL to L recurs in p34-q1-a, and 2000 cm³ to L recurs in p34-q3-b. Neither pair has an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared complete parts and group instructions. The instructions select the same conversions without adding a distinguishing cue or mathematical given. Supplementary-practice provenance does not state a purpose for repeating these exact quantities.
findings.assumptions: The supplied instructions contain the intended purposes of these repetitions.

repair.proposal: Keep the supplementary drill parts. Change p34-q1-a, currently labelled j, to “2400 mL to L”, answer 2.4 L. Change p34-q3-b, currently labelled f, to “6000 cm³ to L”, answer 6 L.

findings.doneWhen: Both later exercise parts retain their conversion structures with different quantities.

findings.finding: Compare two equal water-level drops above the pool's sloping floor.
findings.breakdown: Equal drops remove equal volumes while water still covers the entire rectangular floor footprint.
findings.checked: After both 25 cm drops, the shallow end remains 0.5 m deep. Each removed layer therefore has volume 50 × 25 × 0.25 = 312.5 m³ = 312.5 kL. Only rectangular-prism volume and capacity conversion are needed.
findings.assumptions: Use the existing ideal pool model with vertical sides, a horizontal water surface and a straight sloping floor.

repair.proposal: Append after p40-q20-c: d. Starting with the full pool, how much water is lost when its level drops by 25 cm? Answer: 312.5 kL. e. How much additional water is lost if its level then drops by another 25 cm? Answer: 312.5 kL. f. Explain why these two losses are equal even though the pool has a sloping floor. Expected: each removed layer has horizontal area 50 × 25 m² and thickness 0.25 m.

findings.doneWhen: The three follow-up parts distinguish water-layer volume from the shape of the pool floor.

findings.finding: Connect a triangular prism's side view with its different internal sections.
findings.breakdown: The task asks students to explain why a projected view does not determine every cross-section.
findings.checked: p3 supplies the rectangular side view. p10 explicitly demonstrates rectangular longitudinal sections and triangular sections parallel to the ends. Both proposed section shapes are correct for non-degenerate cuts through the right triangular prism.
findings.assumptions: Cuts pass through the interior; a longitudinal cutting plane is parallel to a rectangular side face.

repair.proposal: After p12-q2, offer: “Return to the triangular prism in p3-example-perspective. Its side view is a rectangle. Must every cross-section also be a rectangle? Give two different section shapes and describe the cutting planes.” Expected answer: No. A cut parallel to a triangular end gives a congruent triangle; an interior longitudinal cut parallel to a rectangular side gives a rectangle. A view projects the solid, whereas a cross-section shows the region exposed by a cut.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task connects views and sections using only the geometry already demonstrated.

findings.finding: All introductory end views appear symmetric, so copying the front view unchanged produces the correct back view without exposing the required left-right reversal. Independent practice then requires that distinction for asymmetric ends.
findings.breakdown: A student using the plausible rule 'the back view is an unchanged copy of the front' would retain the right triangle's vertical leg, the L shape's tall leg or the pentagon's cut-off corner on the wrong side. The first independent question already requires this unmodelled distinction.
findings.checked: Checked all supplied teaching, which is complete. The worked triangle, guided rectangle and guided house profile do not visibly distinguish copying from horizontal reflection. The guided house's solution specification mentions reversal of actual asymmetry, but its approximately symmetric drawing does not demonstrate that contrast. These practice parts are required introductory practice, and their difficulty comes from viewing direction rather than arithmetic.
findings.assumptions: Students have ordinary prior experience of shapes and views; the supplied teaching does not establish how an asymmetric end changes when viewed from behind. Calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before p4-q1-a, add one guided contrast showing an asymmetric triangular end. Have students sketch its front and back views, then explicitly compare the reversed left-right positions while keeping up unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: Guided teaching visibly distinguishes an unchanged copy from the horizontally reflected back view of an asymmetric end.

findings.finding: Isolate the different effects of doubling cylinder height and doubling radius.
findings.breakdown: The existing practice varies dimensions and representations without a controlled comparison of linear and squared dependence.
findings.checked: Using p24's formula gives 12π, 24π, 96π and 192π cm³, with successive factors 2, 4 and 2. The follow-up diameter gives radius 5 cm and volume 175π cm³. All dimensions are positive and both radius and diameter substitution have been taught.
findings.assumptions: Use exact answers in terms of π; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: After p25-q3, add: “Before calculating, predict how each volume compares with the preceding one. Find exact volumes: (a) r = 2 cm, h = 3 cm; (b) r = 2 cm, h = 6 cm; (c) r = 4 cm, h = 6 cm; (d) r = 4 cm, h = 12 cm. What happens when height doubles? When radius doubles?” Expected volumes: 12π, 24π, 96π, 192π cm³. Each transition changes one dimension and holds the other constant. Height doubling doubles volume; radius doubling quadruples it. Follow with: “Find the volume when diameter = 10 cm and height = 7 cm.” Expected answer: 175π cm³.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict and explain the two scaling effects, then solve an unpatterned diameter question.

findings.finding: Explain why two conversion routes from cubic metres to millilitres agree.
findings.breakdown: The task distinguishes cubing a length conversion factor from applying a capacity conversion factor.
findings.checked: p30 supplies the cubic conversion factor, p32 supplies capacity factors and p33 supplies volume-capacity equivalences. Both routes give 1,000,000 mL. Capacity factors already compare complete volumes and must not be cubed.
findings.assumptions: The task concerns equivalent measures of volume, with no container geometry or calculator required.

repair.proposal: After p34-q3, offer: “Convert 1 m³ to mL in two ways: first through cm³, then through kL and L. Explain why cubing 100 is appropriate in the first route, while cubing each capacity factor is inappropriate in the second.” Expected answer: 1 m³ = 100³ cm³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1,000,000 mL; also 1 m³ = 1 kL = 1000 L = 1,000,000 mL. The factor 100 converts each of three lengths; the capacity factors compare complete volumes.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify both equal results and explain which conversion factors require cubing.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review of rectangular-prism and cylinder volume calculation, although both are substantial first steps in its worked examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve and use the appropriate volume formula before applying the recently practised capacity conversions. Conversion practice alone does not rehearse that first step.
findings.checked: p19 and p24 teach the volume formulas, and p29-solids rehearses them two topics earlier. The immediately preceding capacity topic's teaching, guided practice and p34-q3 exercise rehearse conversions, not volume calculation. No review precedes p35-method. The proposed review answers are correct and the four short items fit within one page.
findings.assumptions: The teacher checks the review and responds to recall gaps. Exact cylinder answers avoid dependence on calculator availability.

repair.proposal: Before p35-method, add: “Calculate the volume. Write the formula before substituting. (a) A rectangular prism measuring 5 cm by 3 cm by 8 cm. (b) A rectangular prism with base area 18 m² and height 4 m. (c) A cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 5 cm. (d) A cylinder with radius 2 m and height 7 m. Give cylinder answers in terms of π.” Expected answers: 120 cm³, 72 m³, 45π cm³ and 28π m³.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse both volume calculations before combining them with capacity conversion.
